episodes.title: The Dark History of Seagram: The Mafia, Cults, and Bootlegging Empire
episodes.description:
On the moonless nights of the early 1920s, six-cylinder Buicks and Studebakers rolled south out of Saskatchewan toward the border with North Dakota. The suspensions of these cars had been reinforced with heavy-duty springs, their backseats stripped out to make room for burlap sacks packed with whisky bottles. Chains hung from their rear bumpers, designed to kick up dust and gravel into the faces of any police car foolish enough to try to catch them. The men who dispatched these cars were four brothers named Bronfman — and their family name, in the language of their childhood in Bessarabia, meant liquor. Within a generation, they would build the largest liquor company in the history of the world, buy the most expensive skyscraper ever raised in Manhattan, and befriend every major Mafia boss on the American East Coast. Within another generation, the family fortune would be pouring into a criminal sex cult that branded women with the leader's initials.

In this in-depth, full-length documentary, we explore the century-long arc of Seagram and the Bronfman dynasty — from a Bessarabian tobacco plantation to the largest liquor company on Earth, from the Prohibition-era supply chain that put every major American Mafia family in business with a single Canadian household, to the Mies van der Rohe bronze tower on Park Avenue, to the son who sold DuPont for Universal, to the granddaughters who funded a sex cult that branded women in the basement of a Clifton Park townhouse.

We open in Soroca, Bessarabia, in the late 1880s — Yechiel Bronfman's tobacco plantation on the westernmost edge of the Russian Empire, the 1889 pogroms, and the fugitive name Bronfman that meant "liquor man" in the Yiddish of a household that would eventually make the word literal.

We follow the family through the emigration to Wapella, Saskatchewan in 1889 — the failed homesteading years, the shift into horse trading, the small hotels along the Canadian Pacific Railway, and the frontier hotel-and-liquor economy in which the four Bronfman brothers first served alcohol commercially.

We watch the pivot to medicine — the mail-order whisky trade of the mid-1910s, the 1919 Yorkton mail-order operation, the medicinal alcohol prescriptions written by cooperative doctors, and the way Canadian federal drug policy handed the Bronfman family a legal template for wholesale liquor distribution the moment the United States passed the Volstead Act.

We trace the border boiler operation — the six-cylinder Buicks and Studebakers with reinforced springs, the burlap-sack payloads, the chain-and-gravel evasion tactics, and the murder of Paul Matoff at Bienfait, Saskatchewan on October 4, 1922, the killing that could have destroyed the family and instead consolidated their control of the entire continent-wide bootlegging supply chain.

We reconstruct the client list — Meyer Lansky, Arnold Rothstein, Frank Costello, Charles "Lucky" Luciano, Waxey Gordon, and the Purple Gang of Detroit — the American Mafia bosses whose businesses ran on Bronfman whisky, and the fact that within a decade Sam Bronfman had done more sustained commercial business with the American underworld than any legitimate Canadian executive of the twentieth century.

We follow the 1928 merger with Joseph Seagram & Sons — the Waterloo distillery, the aged-inventory advantage, the transition into the world's largest premium whisky operation, and the December 1933 repeal of Prohibition that Sam Bronfman had spent the previous six years positioning the company to profit from.

We trace the respectability project — Sam Bronfman's re-branding as Mr. Sam, the philanthropy, the World Jewish Congress presidency, the elite Montreal residency, and the two-decade campaign to erase the memory of exactly how the family had come to control the liquor supply of two continents.

We walk into the Seagram Building at 375 Park Avenue in 1958 — Mies van der Rohe and Philip Johnson's bronze-and-glass tower, the most expensive skyscraper per square foot ever raised in Manhattan, the Four Seasons Restaurant in the lobby, and the moment a Canadian bootlegging fortune became the architectural centerpiece of postwar American corporate modernism.

We follow Edgar Bronfman Sr. into the second-generation succession — the 1971 takeover, the DuPont acquisition of 1981 that made Seagram the largest shareholder of the largest chemical company in the United States, and the equity position that anchored the family's wealth through the 1980s and 1990s.
